subject: rosetta-stone
title: The Stone That Cracked a Code
summary: One message in three kinds of writing helped people read hieroglyphs again.

keys.prompt: Why did the Rosetta Stone help people read hieroglyphs?
keys.answer: It had the same message in hieroglyphs and in Greek. Experts could already read the Greek.

options.text: It had the same message in Greek, which experts could read
It came with a list of what each sign meant
A priest had carved how to read the signs

keys.prompt: Why did code-breakers start with the names inside ovals?
keys.answer: A name sounds about the same in any language. So the signs for a name were likely to stand for sounds.

options.text: A name sounds about the same in any language
The ovals had the biggest signs
The ovals were the only part not broken

keys.prompt: What did Champollion figure out about hieroglyphs?
keys.answer: Many signs stand for sounds, like letters. Others stand for a whole word or idea.

options.text: Many signs stand for sounds, and some stand for ideas
Every sign is just a picture of a thing
Each sign stands for a whole sentence

cards.title: A secret note
cards.text: Imagine you find a note in a secret code. Next to it is the same note in English. Could you crack the code? In 1799, people found a stone that gave them a puzzle just like that.

cards.question: The first people to study the stone thought cracking the code would take two weeks. How long did it really take?

options.text: Two weeks
About two years
About 20 years

cards.reveal: About 20 years! The signs were much trickier than anyone expected.

cards.title: One message, three kinds of writing
cards.text: In 196 BC, priests in Egypt wrote a message to honor their king, Ptolemy V. They carved it in three kinds of writing. The top was hieroglyphs. The middle was Demotic, the everyday writing. The bottom was Greek.
cards.example: Hieroglyphs and Demotic were two ways to write the same Egyptian language. It is a bit like fancy writing and everyday handwriting.

cards.title: Found in a wall
cards.text: For about 1,400 years, nobody could read hieroglyphs. Then, in July 1799, French soldiers were fixing an old fort near the town of Rosetta in Egypt. Inside a wall was a broken stone covered in writing. People hoped it was the key.
cards.example: Today the stone is in the British Museum in London. It is the most visited object there.

cards.title: Names in ovals
cards.text: Some hieroglyphs sit inside ovals called cartouches. Thomas Young, a scientist from England, guessed they held kings' names. He found the name Ptolemy and worked out sounds for some of its signs.
cards.example: It is like spotting your own name in a coded note. Now you know a few of the letters!

why.q: Why was a name a good place to start?
why.a: A name like Ptolemy sounds about the same in any language. So its signs were likely to stand for sounds.

cards.title: Re... s... s!
cards.text: In 1822, Jean-François Champollion from France looked at another king's name. It had four signs. The first was a sun. In Coptic, a later form of Egyptian, the word for sun was "re." The last two signs meant "s." Only one name fit: Ramesses!
cards.example: He ran to his brother's office, shouted "I've got it!" and fainted. People first thought the code would take two weeks. It took about 20 years.

why.q: Why was Ramesses a big deal?
why.a: Ramesses was an Egyptian king, not a Greek one. So Egyptians used sound signs for their own words too.

cards.title: Sounds and ideas
cards.text: Hieroglyphs are not only pictures. Some signs stand for sounds, like letters. Others stand for a whole word or idea. Egyptian writing mixes both, even in one word!
cards.example: It is a bit like writing "I ♥ NY." The letters are sounds. The heart means love.

cards.question: Imagine people 3,000 years from now find one of your school notebooks. What clues would help them figure out how to read it?
nudges: What words might show up again and again?
Would your name be a good place to start? Why?

questions.q: What three kinds of writing are on the Rosetta Stone?

options.text: Hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek
English, French and Greek
options.why: English and French are not on it. It was carved in ancient Egypt.

options.text: Only hieroglyphs
options.why: There were three kinds. The Greek part was the big help.

questions.q: Why did the Greek part help so much?

options.text: Experts could still read Greek
options.why: Right. They could read the Greek and compare it to the signs.

options.text: It had a picture next to each sign
options.why: It had no pictures. It helped because people could read it.

options.text: It told people how to read hieroglyphs
options.why: It did not explain the code. It was the same message, so experts could compare.

questions.q: Champollion read the name Ramesses. What did that show?

options.text: Egyptians used sound signs for their own words too
options.why: Yes. Ramesses was an Egyptian king.

options.text: Hieroglyphs are just pictures
options.why: Not quite. The signs in Ramesses stood for sounds.

options.text: Only Greek kings had names in ovals
options.why: Ramesses was an Egyptian king, and his name was in an oval too.

sources.title: How the Rosetta Stone Unlocked the Secrets of Ancient Egypt
sources.supports: Champollion announced the decipherment on September 27, 1822, after bursting into his brother's office on September 14 shouting "I've got it!" and collapsing; the stone was found in July 1799 in a fort wall near Rashid (Rosetta); the 196 B.C.E. decree for Ptolemy V is in hieroglyphs, Demotic (a shorthand form of hieroglyphs) and Greek, two languages in three scripts; Dolnick: the first people expected two weeks, it took 20 years; "a propaganda poster carved in stone"; the versions said "only roughly the same thing, as if three people had each described the same movie"; 14 hieroglyphic lines survive; priests mainly used hieroglyphs, the public Demotic; hieroglyphs fell out of use some 1,400 years earlier; a hybrid system of sound, picture and idea signs ("I ♥ New York"); Young, an English physician and physicist, focused on cartouches because names are pronounced roughly the same in any language, like Chinese spelling foreign names by sound; Young found Ptolemy, published in the Britannica in 1819, and would not accept sound signs beyond foreign names; Champollion used Coptic, written in the Greek alphabet; the four-sign Abu Simbel cartouche of Ramses with a sun (ra or re in Coptic) and a repeated s; British Museum since 1802.

sources.title: Rosetta Stone
sources.supports: Decree of 196 BC for Ptolemy V issued by priests at Memphis in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek; hieroglyphic text in a deliberately archaic neo-Middle Egyptian; found in July 1799 by French soldiers demolishing a wall while strengthening Fort Julien near Rosetta, with hopes it could be the key to hieroglyphs; most visited object in the British Museum; only the last 14 hieroglyphic lines survive; Ptolemy V crowned at 12 amid the Great Theban Revolt and losses abroad, decree just over a year later; Ptolemaic kings needed priestly support; prints and casts circulated in Europe; first Greek translations 1803; Akerblad's 29-letter Demotic alphabet, more than half correct; Young's Ptolemaios; Champollion's Cleopatra reading from the Philae obelisk and public announcement on 27 September 1822; the three versions cannot be matched word for word; last hieroglyphic inscription AD 394.

sources.title: Decipherment of ancient Egyptian scripts
sources.supports: Scripts mix phonetic and ideographic signs; classical authors called hieroglyphs ideographic, which hampered decipherment; Horapollo's goose = 'son' error, really shared consonants; last hieroglyphic text AD 394; Young's eight-sign Ptolemy cartouche and the title 'living for ever, beloved of Ptah'; 13 sound values (6 correct, 3 partly, 4 wrong); about 80 hieroglyph-Demotic matches and 200 hieroglyphic words in his 1819 article; Griffith's verdict on Young's method; Champollion's Ptolemy-Cleopatra cross-check (p, l, o; homophones for t); Ramesses (Coptic re for sun, s-s), Thutmose, and 'birth' = Coptic mise; Lettre read 27 September 1822 with Young in the audience; 1824 Precis quote; Coptic 'like French from Latin'; the ms sign read as m; Lepsius 1837: 30 one-sound signs vs 200+ for Champollion and 24 today; Ray on Young and Demotic; Parkinson's verdict on credit.
